Actions on Objectives
—
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key.
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High

ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"

   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

Flyto2 flyto-verification unauthenticated POST /run on :8344 (CVE-2026-67426 SSRF entry) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound HTTP POST to the /run endpoint of the flyto-verification service on TCP 8344 from non-loopback/remote sources. The shipped Dockerfile binds 0.0.0.0:8344 and /run has no auth dependency, so any remote POST /run is the unauthenticated entry point for the callback_url SSRF and runner-secret exfiltration chain. Rationale: Uses the article's concrete endpoint (POST /run) and the Dockerfile-shipped port 8344 (verification_service.py:363-364, Dockerfile.verification CMD). Restricting to external/remote sources leverages the fix guidance ('bind loopback by default') to separate attack traffic from legit internal callers. Corroborated against the GitLab advisory confirming the 0.0.0.0:8344 exposure. Cross-checked against: • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/ • https://cvereports.com/reports/CVE-2026-67426
ATT&CKT1190 T1133
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate internal verification jobs POSTing /run from an app tier reachable via a public NAT egress IP
  • Vulnerability scanners / ASM tools probing the /run path on 8344
  • Load-balancer or uptime health checks hitting /run
  • Developer testing the verification service from a bastion/VPN with a public source IP
Suppression filter
| where not(SourceIP in ("<known-healthcheck-ip>"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the source IP is external and not an expected internal caller; pull the full request (body should contain callback_url/workflowYaml) from app or proxy logs and check whether the host is running flyto-core <= 2.26.6. 2) Contain: rebind flyto-verification to loopback (or firewall 8344 to internal only), and rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET immediately since it may already be exfiltrated. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC2/UC3 — search for outbound connections from the verification host to 169.254.169.254 or to any public IP, and audit engine-callback authentications using the (now-possibly-leaked) runner secret.
DeviceNetworkEvents

| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort == 8344
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, LocalPort, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DestinationPort == 8344
| where RequestMethod == "POST"
| where RequestURL has "/run"
| where isnotempty(SourceIP) and not(SourceIP startswith "10." or SourceIP startswith "192.168." or SourceIP startswith "172.16." or SourceIP startswith "127.")
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, DestinationIP, DestinationPort, RequestMethod, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct
| order by TimeGenerated desc

flyto-verification SSRF to cloud metadata IP (169.254.169.254) — runner-secret/IMDS theft AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts outbound connections from the flyto-verification runner (python/uvicorn/gunicorn/flyto-verification) to cloud instance-metadata endpoints (169.254.169.254, 100.100.100.200, metadata.google.internal). CVE-2026-67426's callback_url bypasses the target_allowed allowlist and SSRF guard, letting an attacker force the service to POST to the IMDS with a controlled body and harvest instance credentials. Rationale: The article explicitly names 'cloud-metadata IP' as an SSRF target; MITRE T1552.005 and Elastic's prebuilt IMDS-SSRF rule confirm 169.254.169.254 (plus Alibaba 100.100.100.200 / GCP metadata.google.internal) as the canonical endpoints. Scoping to the python/flyto-verification process removes legit cloud-agent IMDS calls, making a web-runner->IMDS connection a near-zero-FP signal. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1552/005/ • https://www.elastic.co/docs/reference/security/prebuilt-rules/rules/cross-platform/credential_access_web_server_cloud_imds_ssrf_request • https://advisories.gitlab.com/pypi/flyto-core/CVE-2026-67426/
ATT&CKT1552.005 T1190
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A legitimate flyto workflow that intentionally targets an internal 169.254.x host as a callback (rare/misconfig)
  • Cloud SDK embedded in the same python venv making a genuine IMDSv2 token call for the app's own role
  • Security testing / red-team validation of the SSRF fix
  • Sidecar or observability agent sharing the process name 'python' reaching metadata for instance tags
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("flyto", "verification")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the initiating process is the flyto-verification runner and capture the destination path/body; check IMDS access logs (if IMDSv2 enabled) for a token issuance from this host at the same time. 2) Contain: rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET and any instance-role credentials that IMDS could have returned; enforce IMDSv2 (HttpTokens=required) and block 169.254.0.0/16 egress from the container; upgrade flyto-core to 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: search CloudTrail/AAD/GCP audit for use of the instance-role or managed-identity credentials from unexpected IPs shortly after this event, and check UC3 for the secret being POSTed to an external attacker host.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where RemoteIP in ("169.254.169.254", "100.100.100.200") or RemoteUrl has "metadata.google.internal"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn", "flyto-verification", "flyto")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where DstIpAddr in ("169.254.169.254", "100.100.100.200") or DstHostname has "metadata.google.internal"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber, NetworkApplicationProtocol, Url
| order by TimeGenerated desc

flyto-verification runner egress to external public host — FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET exfiltration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the flyto-verification/python runner initiating outbound connections to public (non-RFC1918, non-link-local) destinations. Because callback_url is attacker-controlled and the service unconditionally attaches X-Internal-Key: $FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, any egress from this backend runner to an arbitrary internet host is a candidate secret-exfiltration callback. Rationale: Grounded in the sink from the advisory: post_callback -> session.post(callback_url, headers={'X-Internal-Key': FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET}) (verification_service.py:330-335). A backend verification runner that is only supposed to call the internal engine should never egress to a public IP, so process-scoped public egress is a high-value exfiltration hunt for the leaked runner secret. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-jx74-cqjv-2c67 • https://cvefeed.io/vuln/detail/CVE-2026-67428
ATT&CKT1567 T1552
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate engine callback endpoint hosted on a public IP / SaaS domain rather than internal
  • Python dependency/package fetches (pip, telemetry SDKs) from the same runner venv
  • Outbound calls to a public webhook/notification service used by real workflows
  • CDN or object-storage uploads the workflow performs as designed
Suppression filter
| where RemoteUrl !has "pypi.org" and RemoteUrl !has "pythonhosted.org"
Response runbook
1) Triage: resolve the public RemoteIP/RemoteUrl and compare against the documented internal engine callback host; if it is unknown/attacker-looking, capture the flow and any TLS SNI. 2) Contain: block egress from the flyto-verification container except to the known engine, rotate FLYTO_RUNNER_SECRET, and upgrade to flyto-core 2.26.7. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1 (inbound POST /run carrying that callback_url) and UC2 (IMDS access), and review engine-callback auth logs for forged authenticated callbacks using the leaked X-Internal-Key.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("flyto-verification", "flyto")) or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("python", "python3", "uvicorn", "gunicorn") and InitiatingProcessCommandLine has "flyto")
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), Count=count(), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen desc

OctLurk deployment via 'GoogleUpDate' scheduled task launching Videos\1.bat AIInstallation High
Hunts the OctLurk/LurkProxy deployment step where the actor creates a scheduled task named GoogleUpDate that runs a staging batch script from the user's Videos or Desktop folder to install the loader service. Anchored on the exact task name, batch paths and the two published batch-script MD5s. Rationale: Uses the verbatim task name 'GoogleUpDate' from the article code block, the exact staging paths C:\Users\<user>\Videos\1.bat and Desktop\auto.bat, and the two published batch MD5s (6ecf84... and b874123...) — all attacker-chosen, high-fidelity strings. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Google Update/Chrome update scheduled tasks named 'GoogleUpdateTaskMachine' (note different casing/spacing — GoogleUpDate is the impostor)
  • Admin-authored batch scripts stored under a user's Videos or Desktop folder for ad-hoc automation
  • Software-deployment tooling that stages .bat files on Desktop before running
  • Pen-test/red-team tooling using schtasks for lateral execution
Suppression filter
| where not (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpdateTaskMachine")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full DeviceProcessEvents tree on the host — confirm the task ran as SYSTEM immediately after creation and whether it invoked sc.exe/1.bat to create a service (NgcCIntSvc/Cusrxsrv/etc.). 2) Contain: delete the GoogleUpDate task, isolate the host, and capture the referenced .bat and any DLL it drops for hashing against the loader IOCs. 3) Hunt: sweep for the loader service names and C2 domain dns.multitoconference.com across the estate; check which admin account created the task (remote creation implies stolen creds).
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (FileName =~ "schtasks.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Videos\1.bat"
    or ProcessCommandLine has @"\Desktop\auto.bat"
    or MD5 in ("6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a","b874123a80fc4f40e06872b9cb54ebc6")
    or InitiatingProcessMD5 in ("6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a","b874123a80fc4f40e06872b9cb54ebc6")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\schtasks.exe" and CommandLine has "GoogleUpDate")
    or CommandLine has @"\Videos\1.bat"
    or CommandLine has @"\Desktop\auto.bat"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/LurkProxy loader service registration (ServiceMain=RegisterService loading oleasapi.dll/msbasesysdc.dll) AIInstallation High
Hunts the loader install step where a service is created whose ServiceMain parameter is set to the export 'RegisterService' and whose ServiceDll is one of the named loader DLLs. Covers the custom loader execution/payload-decryption stage flagged by the reviewer. Rationale: Anchors on the article's distinctive loader mechanics: ServiceMain param pointing at the non-standard export 'RegisterService', the exact loader DLL names oleasapi.dll (MD5 082d49ef...) and msbasesysdc.dll, and the attacker-chosen service names. Legit service DLLs almost never store 'RegisterService' as ServiceMain. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1543.003 T1055.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry Endpoint.Services
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Hyper-V integration services (vmicvss, vmictimesync) — note the impostor is vmictimerosync/vmicagent with altered spelling
  • Genuine PNRPHostSvc / peer-networking service reconfiguration (excluded from the name list for this reason)
  • Third-party service-DLL products that legitimately set a custom ServiceMain export name
  • Backup/EDR agents re-registering service DLLs during upgrade
Suppression filter
| where not (RegistryKey has @"\Services\vmictimesync" or RegistryKey has @"\Services\vmicvss")
Response runbook
1) Triage: on the flagged host dump the service registry key and the referenced DLL; hash it against 082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069 and check for the RegisterService/Refresh exports. 2) Contain: stop and delete the malicious service, isolate the host, and preserve the DLL and the C: volume serial (used as loader XOR key-2). 3) Hunt: pivot from the DLL to svchost network connections toward the LurkProxy/OctLurk C2 IPs and to any GoogleUpDate task; sweep other hosts for the same service names.
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RegistryKey has @"\Services\"
| where (RegistryValueName =~ "ServiceMain" and RegistryValueData =~ "RegisterService")
    or (RegistryValueName in~ ("ServiceDll","ImagePath") and RegistryValueData has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll"))
    or RegistryKey has_any (@"\Services\NgcCIntSvc", @"\Services\Cusrxsrv", @"\Services\specitsrc", @"\Services\cmtastsvc", @"\Services\vmictimerosync", @"\Services\vmicagent")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RegistryKey, RegistryValueName, RegistryValueData, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4697
| where ServiceFileName has_any ("oleasapi.dll","msbasesysdc.dll")
    or ServiceName in~ ("NgcCIntSvc","Cusrxsrv","specitsrc","cmtastsvc","vmictimerosync","vmicagent")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ServiceName, ServiceFileName, ServiceType, ServiceStartType
| order by TimeGenerated desc

OctLurk/SilkLurk/LurkProxy C2 beacon to named backdoor infrastructure AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts host communication with the published OctLurk, SilkLurk and LurkProxy C2 domains and IP addresses (many on dynamic-DNS providers, backdoor sockets on TCP/443). High-fidelity IOC match tying an endpoint to the campaign's command-and-control. Rationale: Direct match on the article's Indicators-of-Compromise section: 15 C2 domains (incl. dynamic-DNS gleeze.com/kozow.com/casacam.net/accesscam.org used by the backdoors) and 11 C2 IPs, including dns.multitoconference.com (OctLurk, TCP/443) and 154.196.162.76 (LurkProxy). Projecting InitiatingProcessFileName surfaces the svchost/service host that beacons. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1568.002
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • digital.leroymerlin.com is a lookalike of a real retailer domain — a genuine visit to the retailer's real domain will not match this exact FQDN, but analysts may confuse the two
  • Security scanners / TI-enrichment sandboxes deliberately resolving IOC domains
  • Threat-intel researchers detonating samples in the same tenant
  • Recycled dynamic-DNS hostnames later re-registered by benign users (low, but possible for gleeze/kozow subdomains)
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the initiating process on the beaconing host — expect svchost.exe hosting a malicious service DLL rather than a browser. 2) Contain: block the domains/IPs at egress and DNS sinkhole, isolate the host. 3) Hunt: from the host pivot to the loader service (UC2) and GoogleUpDate task (UC1), pull all other internal hosts resolving the same DDNS providers, and review any Impacket/FSCAN activity that may have followed C2 established.

OctLurk victim-fingerprinting recon command burst (chcp 1256 + qwinsta + klist + tasklist) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the post-compromise fingerprinting sequence OctLurk runs through its command shell plugin: switching the code page to 1256 (Arabic), enumerating sessions with qwinsta, listing Kerberos logon sessions with klist sessions, and running TASKLIST /V — several fired from one parent within minutes. Rationale: Built from the article's exact fingerprinting command table (chcp 1256, powershell $PSVersionTable, qwinsta, klist sessions, TASKLIST /V). chcp 1256 (Arabic code page, matching the Syrian/MoFA victimology) plus the burst of session/process discovery from a single parent within 10 minutes is far more specific than any single LOLBin. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1082 T1057 T1033
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk/sysadmin interactively troubleshooting RDP sessions (qwinsta) and Kerberos (klist) on a server
  • Logon scripts that call chcp for localization on Arabic-locale endpoints
  • Monitoring/inventory agents running tasklist /V periodically
  • PowerShell profiling scripts querying $PSVersionTable during onboarding
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("mmc.exe","explorer.exe","taskmgr.exe","ScreenConnect.WindowsClient.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process of the command burst — a cmd.exe spawned by svchost/an unknown service DLL (not an interactive shell) strongly indicates the OctLurk command-shell plugin. 2) Contain: if parent is a suspicious service host, isolate and capture the DLL. 3) Hunt: correlate the same host/timeframe with C2 beacons (UC3) and follow-on credential dumping (UC5) or FSCAN (UC6); check whether chcp 1256 aligns with Arabic-language victim targeting.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where (FileName =~ "chcp.com" and ProcessCommandLine has "1256")
    or FileName =~ "qwinsta.exe"
    or (FileName =~ "klist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "sessions")
    or (FileName =~ "tasklist.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/V")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize CmdCount=dcount(FileName), Cmds=make_set(ProcessCommandLine, 10), StartTime=min(Timestamp), EndTime=max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessId, InitiatingProcessFileName, bin(Timestamp, 10m)
| where CmdCount >= 3
| order by StartTime desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "\\chcp.com" and CommandLine has "1256")
    or NewProcessName endswith "\\qwinsta.exe"
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\klist.exe" and CommandLine has "sessions")
    or (NewProcessName endswith "\\tasklist.exe" and CommandLine has "/V")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has "$PSVersionTable")
| summarize CmdCount=dcount(NewProcessName), Cmds=make_set(CommandLine, 10), StartTime=min(TimeGenerated), EndTime=max(TimeGenerated)
    by Computer, SubjectUserName, ProcessId, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)
| where CmdCount >= 3
| order by StartTime desc
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 (@CommandLine:*"chcp 1256"* OR @Image:(*\qwinsta.exe OR *\Qwinsta.exe) OR @CommandLine:*"klist sessions"* OR @CommandLine:*"TASKLIST /V"* OR @CommandLine:*PSVersionTable*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/chcp\s+1256|klist\s+sessions|tasklist\s+\/v|\$PSVersionTable/i OR ImageFileName=/\\qwinsta\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName], function=count(field=ImageFileName, distinct=true))
| _count >= 3
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process) as cmds dc(Processes.process_name) as cmdcount min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chcp.com AND Processes.process="*1256*") OR Processes.process_name=qwinsta.exe OR (Processes.process_name=klist.exe AND Processes.process="*sessions*") OR (Processes.process_name=tasklist.exe AND Processes.process="*/V*") OR (Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe,pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*PSVersionTable*") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_id Processes.parent_process_name _time span=10m | where cmdcount>=3 | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process) as cmds dc(Processes.process_name) as cmdcount min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=chcp.com AND Processes.process="*1256*") OR Processes.process_name=qwinsta.exe OR (Processes.process_name=klist.exe AND Processes.process="*sessions*") OR (Processes.process_name=tasklist.exe AND Processes.process="*/V*") OR (Processes.process_name IN (powershell.exe,pwsh.exe) AND Processes.process="*PSVersionTable*") by Processes.dest Processes.parent_process_id Processes.parent_process_name _time span=10m | where cmdcount>=3 | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Impacket secretsdump credential dumping in OctLurk post-compromise AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts execution of Impacket's secretsdump used by the actor for credential dumping (SAM/LSA/NTDS) during lateral movement. Detects the secretsdump invocation and its DCSync-style '-just-dc' argument pattern regardless of interpreter or compiled packaging. Rationale: The article explicitly lists 'Impacket — secretsdump' in post-compromise credential harvesting. Anchoring on the module name and the DCSync-style '-just-dc ...@target' argument shape catches both python and compiled/renamed Impacket packaging without relying on a hash the report says was unavailable. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1003.002 T1003.006
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red-team / authorized penetration tests running Impacket secretsdump
  • AD migration or password-audit tooling that legitimately performs DCSync
  • Security researchers testing Impacket in a lab within the same tenant
  • Backup solutions invoking ntds util (different arg shape — should not match '-just-dc @')
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("svc-adaudit","svc-pwaudit")
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full command line and the account context; confirm whether '-just-dc' (DCSync against a DC) or SAM/LSA local dump, and whether the target host is a domain controller. 2) Contain: isolate source host, force-reset any exposed krbtgt/privileged and service accounts, and revoke Kerberos tickets if DCSync succeeded. 3) Hunt: correlate with UC1/UC2 loader presence and UC3 C2 on the same host; look for FSCAN recon (UC6) that preceded the credential dump and unusual admin logons to the DC.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("secretsdump","secretsdump.py")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "-just-dc" and ProcessCommandLine has "@")
    or (ProcessCommandLine has "-just-dc-ntlm" and ProcessCommandLine has "-hashes")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has_any ("secretsdump","secretsdump.py")
    or (CommandLine has "-just-dc" and CommandLine has "@")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Impacket secretsdump credential dumping

FSCAN internal network reconnaissance fan-out AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the internal reconnaissance stage where the actor runs FSCAN to sweep the network — one source touching many internal hosts across scanner ports (SSH, SMB, RDP, MSSQL, MySQL, Redis) in a short window, plus direct fscan binary execution. Rationale: The article names 'Network scan: FSCAN' as post-compromise activity. Detection combines the direct fscan.exe process (Sigma) with the behavioral fan-out (one internal source hitting >=50 hosts on FSCAN's default scan ports within 5 min), which survives binary renaming. Sentinel query fixed to group on SourceIP/SourceHostName (valid CommonSecurityLog columns) instead of the non-existent DeviceName. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1046 T1018
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorized vulnerability scanners (Nessus, Qualys, OpenVAS) sweeping the estate
  • Network/asset-discovery tools (Lansweeper, nmap-based inventory)
  • SCCM/endpoint-management client-push connectivity checks across a subnet
  • Backup or monitoring servers probing SMB/SQL on many hosts
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ ("scanner01","nessus01","lansweeper01") and InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("nessus-service.exe","nmap.exe","Nessus.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the scanning process (InitiatingProcessFileName / ContextImageFileName) and whether the source host is an approved scanner; an unknown/renamed binary spawned by a service host is high-signal for FSCAN. 2) Contain: isolate the source host and block its lateral SMB/RDP/SQL traffic. 3) Hunt: correlate with the loader (UC2), C2 (UC3) and any subsequent secretsdump (UC5); map which internal hosts responded on 445/3389 to scope likely lateral targets.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| where RemotePort in (22, 135, 139, 445, 1433, 3306, 3389, 6379)
| summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(RemoteIP), Ports=make_set(RemotePort, 20), StartTime=min(Timestamp), EndTime=max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessId, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where DistinctHosts >= 50   // fscan-style fan-out; tune to /24 estate size
| order by DistinctHosts desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationPort in (22, 135, 139, 445, 1433, 3306, 3389, 6379)
| summarize DistinctHosts=dcount(DestinationIP), Ports=make_set(DestinationPort, 20), StartTime=min(TimeGenerated), EndTime=max(TimeGenerated)
    by SourceIP, SourceHostName, bin(TimeGenerated, 5m)
| where DistinctHosts >= 50   // fscan-style fan-out; tune to estate size
| order by DistinctHosts desc
title: FSCAN network scanner binary execution

Browser credential-store theft via OctLurk browser password decryptor AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the OctLurk 'Browser Password Decryptor' capability: a non-browser process reading Chromium/Edge 'Login Data' and 'Local State' (AES key) or Firefox 'logins.json'/'key4.db' to steal stored passwords. Rationale: The article lists 'Browser Password Decryptor' / browser password stealer as an OctLurk capability. High-fidelity signal is a non-browser process touching the Chromium 'Login Data' + 'Local State' pair (Local State holds the DPAPI-wrapped AES key) or Firefox key4.db/logins.json — the exact files any browser-credential stealer must read. Datadog/CloudWatch left empty as browser file-read telemetry isn't in their standard sources. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/octlurk-silklurk-backdoors-central-asia/120840/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup/sync agents (OneDrive, Google Drive, corporate backup) copying user profile directories
  • Endpoint DLP or forensic tools inventorying browser artifacts
  • Browser migration/import utilities reading another browser's profile
  • Antivirus on-access scans opening the SQLite stores
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("OneDrive.exe","googledrivesync.exe","Dropbox.exe","MsMpEng.exe","code.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the accessing process and its parent; a process from an unusual path or a service host reading both Login Data and Local State is a strong stealer indicator. 2) Contain: isolate the host and force password resets for accounts whose credentials are likely stored in that browser profile (prioritize privileged/SSO). 3) Hunt: correlate with OctLurk loader/C2 on the same host, look for archive utilities (WinRAR/7z) staging the harvested data, and check for outbound transfer to the C2 IPs.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Local State","logins.json","key4.db","Web Data","cookies.sqlite")
    or FolderPath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Login Data", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","msedgewebview2.exe","OneDrive.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ActionType
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\User Data\Default\Login Data", @"\User Data\Local State", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
    or TargetFileName in~ ("key4.db","logins.json","Login Data","Local State")
| where not(ActingProcessName has_any ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe","msedgewebview2.exe"))
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Non-browser access to browser credential stores

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Service install for persistence — sc.exe / new service registry write Installation High
Service install with binPath pointing to user-writeable path or LOLBin. Detects via process telemetry (sc.exe create) and registry (HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Services\* writes).
ATT&CKT1543.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Registry DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName =~ "sc.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "create"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
// EventID 4697 is "Service installed" — direct signal, no cmdline-regex needed.
union
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4697
        | where SubjectUserName !endswith "$"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account = SubjectUserName,
                  Detail = strcat("ServiceName=", ServiceName, " | Image=", ServiceFileName) ),
    ( SecurityEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where EventID == 4688
        | where Account !endswith "$"
        | where NewProcessName endswith "\sc.exe" and CommandLine has "create"
        | where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(\Users\|\AppData\|\ProgramData\|\Temp\)"
        | project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account,
                  Detail = strcat("4688 sc.exe create: ", CommandLine) )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) Exploitation High
Browser-pasted PowerShell launched from explorer/Run dialog — ClickFix social engineering.
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\explorer.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\RuntimeBroker.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(iex|invoke-expression|frombase64|downloadstring|hxxp|curl |wget )"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: FakeCaptcha / ClickFix - Clipboard-Injected PowerShell from Explorer
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d06
status: experimental
description: |
    "FakeCaptcha" / "ClickFix" social-engineering: malicious site asks
    user to press Win+R and paste a payload. The result is
    powershell/mshta launched directly from explorer.exe with iex /
    base64 / downloadstring in the command line.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1204.002
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\explorer.exe'
            - '\RuntimeBroker.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
    selection_cmd:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - 'iex'
            - 'invoke-expression'
            - 'frombase64'
            - 'downloadstring'
            - 'hxxp'
            - 'curl '
            - 'wget '
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child and selection_cmd
falsepositives:
    - IT-driven scripted automation that admins paste-launch
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("explorer.exe","RuntimeBroker.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","mshta.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*iex*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*hxxp*" OR Processes.process="*curl*" OR Processes.process="*wget*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high

Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"

    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"

    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`

// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["082d49ef9f14e6811d68c7e0e82e5069", "f4578e869a735cfad691f927bae3e638", "7c2f64461bb519c6cbf1fc687675514c", "8269d6ba1b6842f9152c90cf7add9b93", "3c9a1ba8e0c7475706adc6376e9d7b7c", "ef59aad625eebda8650aec5820d6ce69", "a0cc7accc79abb0287aaba825d0351f0", "a56cce62930a6bee80d679b4c495a340", "1415a78b75de7db4ba3d1e61d7db4501", "a4d550a3ba0cd073fe3839b99d98a7a8", "32a5985543433a4f60da2fafd873b927", "2a571f6cee42a17d873f4c942649813f", "37dc84e4bcad92fa28f1e7778d088283", "cf903e4a1629aa0582fd0363b5786676", "18dc8bff47cc282508354771d0c8cf8c", "9a1dd1d96481d61934dcc2d568971d06", "6ecf84fb18f6747ed08d7598364d853a", "b874123a80fc4f40e06872b9cb54ebc6", "45cf5916fab4272a1313c26e67aa9220", "4e6d5c4770d5a822d7fcce6a74f7ad73", "5e26df131ff0a679a0a2699b723b46e3"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → [LLM] Autonomous mass-scan burst: langflow_poc.py multi-threaded FOFA target sweep · Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Langflow CVE-2026-33017 unauthenticated RCE exploitation (build_public_tmp) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Chinese-Speaking Threat Actor Harnesses AI Models for Autonomous Cyberattacks
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Hermes Agent autonomous attack framework execution (fofoapi.py / FofaMap MCP) · [LLM] AI coding-tool anti-attribution / permission-bypass config artifacts
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Egress to AI-tool anonymizing proxy code.newcli[.]com (knaithe/KnYuan campaign) · [LLM] Direct egress to Chinese-market LLM APIs (DeepSeek/Qwen) from the estate · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs
Egress to AI-tool anonymizing proxy code.newcli[.]com (knaithe/KnYuan campaign) AICommand & Control High
Hunts outbound connections/DNS to code.newcli[.]com, the third-party proxy the actor used to front Claude Code (/ultra) and Codex (/codex/v1) traffic and reduce traceability. Any estate host resolving or connecting to this domain is either the actor's tooling host or a compromised relay. Rationale: code.newcli[.]com is a hard IOC named in Table 1 as the proxy fronting both Western AI tools; the /ultra and /codex/v1 sub-paths are actor-specific. Very low FP as this is not a mainstream service. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1090.003 T1071.001

  • Sandbox/detonation VM fetching the domain during malware analysis

| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","SenseIR.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Identify the initiating process/user on the host that resolved code.newcli[.]com — legitimate AI-coding tools do not route through this proxy. 2) CONTAIN: Block newcli.com at the proxy/firewall and isolate the host if the process is an unsanctioned agent framework (python, node, hermes). 3) HUNT: Pivot on the same host for egress to api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com, and for langflow_poc.py / fofoapi.py execution to confirm the autonomous-attack tooling.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "newcli.com" or RemoteUrl has_any ("code.newcli.com/ultra","code.newcli.com/codex")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DestinationHostName has "newcli.com" or RequestURL has "code.newcli.com"
| project TimeGenerated, SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName, RequestURL, RequestClientApplication, DeviceVendor, DeviceProduct, DeviceAction
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Direct egress to Chinese-market LLM APIs (DeepSeek/Qwen) from the estate AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts direct API calls to api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com, the native endpoints the actor hit directly (bypassing the proxy) for DeepSeek and Qwen/GLM/Kimi/MiniMax reasoning. Non-developer estate hosts reaching these are candidate autonomous-attack operator nodes. Rationale: api.deepseek[.]com and dashscope.aliyuncs[.]com are the exact native API endpoints in Table 1 the actor used directly. FP medium because legitimate developers may evaluate these models — pivot on non-dev hosts and pair with tooling process names. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic Network_Resolution.DNS

  • Developers or data-science teams legitimately trialing DeepSeek/Qwen APIs
  • AI gateway/enterprise proxy that aggregates multiple model providers
  • Marketing/research staff using consumer AI chat clients
  • CI pipeline calling a model API for code assistance
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msedge.exe","chrome.exe","firefox.exe")
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine whether the host belongs to a sanctioned developer/data-science group and whether the initiating process is a browser vs a scripting/agent runtime (python/node). 2) CONTAIN: If the host is a server or non-dev endpoint running an agent framework, isolate and revoke any local API keys found. 3) HUNT: Correlate with code.newcli[.]com egress, langflow_poc.py/fofoapi.py execution and outbound FOFA queries to confirm autonomous-operator activity vs benign model use.

| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.deepseek.com","dashscope.aliyuncs.com")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Conns=count(), Procs=make_set(InitiatingProcessFileName,10) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl
| order by FirstSeen desc

| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Hits=count() by SourceIP, SourceHostName, DestinationHostName
| order by FirstSeen desc

Langflow CVE-2026-33017 unauthenticated RCE exploitation (build_public_tmp) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts inbound exploitation of Langflow's unauthenticated code-execution surface (CVE-2026-33017, CVSS 9.8) against internet-facing Langflow instances the campaign enumerated via FOFA title="Langflow". Targets POST traffic to the Langflow code-validation API and mass-scan patterns from the actor's langflow_poc.py. Rationale: Grounded in the article's Langflow phase: FOFA title="Langflow", langflow_poc.py scanner and CVE-2026-33017 (CVSS 9.8). Endpoint /api/v1/validate/code is Langflow's documented unauthenticated code-execution surface; note in rationale it is derived from Langflow CVE knowledge, not verbatim from the article which did not print the path. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://github.com/oscar-mine/CVE-2026-33017-Exploit
ATT&CKT1190
Data sourcesWeb.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Langflow users saving/validating custom Python components via the UI
  • Internal QA/regression tests exercising the Langflow API
  • Authenticated automation pipelines building flows programmatically
  • Vulnerability scanners (Nessus/Qualys) safe-checking the endpoint
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the Langflow instance version (1.3.4 was vulnerable per the article) and whether auto_login or a public flow ID is enabled — the exploit only succeeds with those prerequisites. 2) CONTAIN: Put Langflow behind authentication, disable auto_login, and block the scanning source IPs at the WAF. 3) HUNT: Review web logs for the same source IP fingerprint hitting many hosts rapidly (mass FOFA-enumerated scan), and check the Langflow host for post-exploit child processes spawned by the app runtime.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteUrl has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, LocalIP, RemoteIP, RemoteUrl, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where csMethod == "POST" and csUriStem has "/api/v1/validate/code"
| summarize Hits=count(), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), UAs=make_set(csUserAgent,10) by Computer, cIP, csUriStem
| where Hits >= 1
| order by Hits desc

Hermes Agent autonomous attack framework execution (fofoapi.py / FofaMap MCP) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts execution of the actor's autonomous offensive tooling on estate hosts: the Hermes Agent framework and its custom fofoapi.py FOFA-enumeration script / FofaMap-Platinum MCP server driving DeepSeek. Catches the operator node itself rather than the victim. Rationale: fofoapi.py, fofa-cyberspace-search, FofaMap-Platinum-Full-Expert MCP, web-terminal-exploitation and godmode are custom, campaign-unique skill/script names from the Technical Analysis section — extremely low chance of benign collision. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1059.006 T1106
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Red team or purple team replaying the Hermes Agent tooling in a sanctioned exercise
  • Security researcher analyzing the recovered toolset in a lab
  • Threat-intel analyst naming files after the IOCs during investigation
  • A benign unrelated project coincidentally naming a script 'fofoapi.py' (rare)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the host is not a sanctioned red-team box; capture the full command line, parent process and user. 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, snapshot memory/disk, and pull any Hermes Agent config/session logs and Telegram C2 tokens for IR. 3) HUNT: Enumerate the host's home directory for an exposed file server (the article's OPSEC failure), and pivot on outbound FOFA queries, DeepSeek/Qwen API egress and code.newcli[.]com traffic.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("fofoapi.py","fofa-cyberspace-search","FofaMap-Platinum","web-terminal-exploitation","godmode")
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)hermes[-_ ]?agent"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("fofoapi.py","fofa-cyberspace-search","FofaMap-Platinum","web-terminal-exploitation") or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)hermes[-_ ]?agent"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

AI coding-tool anti-attribution / permission-bypass config artifacts AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the actor's tell-tale AI-tool hardening: disabling attribution headers and response storage and forcing auto-approval so the agents run unattended. Detects the specific config keys and CLI flags (CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER=0, disable_response_storage=true, dangerously-skip-permissions, approvalMode yolo) on estate hosts. Rationale: These are verbatim config keys/flags from Table 1 and the Tool Configuration section (CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER:0, CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC:1, disable_response_storage=true, dangerously-skip-permissions:true, approvalMode:yolo). Medium FP because a careless developer could set some of these; the combination or presence on a non-dev host is high-fidelity. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/
ATT&CKT1562.001 T1070
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A developer legitimately running Claude Code with --dangerously-skip-permissions for a trusted local task
  • CI automation setting approvalMode to a non-interactive value
  • Privacy-conscious user disabling telemetry/response storage
  • AI-tool documentation or tutorial commands copy-pasted into a shell
Suppression filter
| where DeviceName !in~ () or isnotempty(DeviceName)
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Determine which AI tool set the flag, the user, and whether the host is a sanctioned developer machine. 2) CONTAIN: If unsanctioned, isolate the host and preserve the tool config directories (.claude, codex config, qwen config) plus any 'trusted directory' allowlists. 3) HUNT: Correlate with code.newcli[.]com and DeepSeek/Qwen egress and with Hermes Agent / fofoapi.py execution to distinguish a careless dev from the autonomous-attack operator.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("dangerously-skip-permissions","CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","disable_response_storage")
   or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)approvalMode\s*[:=]\s*.?yolo"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("dangerously-skip-permissions","CLAUDE_CODE_ATTRIBUTION_HEADER","CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC","disable_response_storage") or ActingProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)approvalMode\s*[:=]\s*.?yolo"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Autonomous mass-scan burst: langflow_poc.py multi-threaded FOFA target sweep AIReconnaissance Medium
Hunts the discovery/scanning phase where the Hermes Agent ran langflow_poc.py against a FOFA-enumerated target file at high concurrency (--scan-file langflow_targets.txt --threads 10). Detects the scanner process and the resulting rapid outbound connection burst characteristic of automated, not human-paced, probing. Rationale: langflow_poc.py, langflow_targets.txt and the --scan-file/--threads 10 flags are the exact command from the Langflow phase; combining the process identity with a public-target fan-out burst (>=10 distinct targets/5m matching the --threads 10 concurrency) separates automated scanning from human pacing. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/autonomous-ai-cyber-attack-campaign/ • https://github.com/oscar-mine/CVE-2026-33017-Exploit
ATT&CKT1595.002 T1046
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned internal vulnerability scanning of Langflow assets by the AppSec team
  • A pentester running the public PoC during an authorized engagement
  • Asset-inventory tooling probing internal Langflow ports (7860)
  • Load testing of a Langflow deployment generating many concurrent connections
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
Response runbook
1) TRIAGE: Confirm the scanning host is not sanctioned scanning infrastructure and review the command line and target file contents (langflow_targets.txt). 2) CONTAIN: Isolate the host, block its outbound scanning, and preserve the target list and PoC binary for scope assessment. 3) HUNT: Enrich the target IPs to find which are your own internet-facing Langflow instances, then check those instances for successful POST /api/v1/validate/code exploitation and post-exploit child processes.
let ScannerHosts = DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "langflow_poc.py" or ProcessCommandLine has "langflow_targets.txt" or (ProcessCommandLine has "--scan-file" and ProcessCommandLine has "--threads")
| distinct DeviceId;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where DeviceId in (ScannerHosts)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and RemotePort in (7860, 80, 443)
| summarize DistinctTargets=dcount(RemoteIP), Conns=count(), Window=max(Timestamp)-min(Timestamp) by DeviceId, DeviceName, bin(Timestamp, 5m)
| where DistinctTargets >= 10   // 10 = actor's --threads 10 concurrency against many FOFA targets in a tight window
| order by DistinctTargets desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has "langflow_poc.py" or ActingProcessCommandLine has "langflow_targets.txt" or (ActingProcessCommandLine has "--scan-file" and ActingProcessCommandLine has "--threads")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01

references:

            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'

Securelist (Kaspersky)
2026-07-30 16 use cases 5 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected
